item.title: How I Got Postgres into a Single Binary
item.description: What if we had full PostreSQL but in the shape of SQLite?
item.content:encoded:
SQLite, but Postgres

SQLite is one of my favorite database technologies. It's a full SQL database, designed as an embeddable library, that stores all its data in a single file. The sqlite3 command line tool is great too. You point it at a file and run queries. There's no server to run.

At the other end of the spectrum is Postgres. It's the most capable general purpose SQL database, trusted in production at scale, and is something of an industry standard. With that comes complexity, starting with the fact that it's client-server.

SQLite is a natural fit for software that needs a database but isn't meant to be deployed in the cloud at scale: desktop apps, self-hosted tools, things you run locally. These applications can use SQLite and manage it themselves, so you barely know there's a database involved.

So when you find self-hostable open source software you'd like to run on your own computer, it can be daunting when it says it requires Postgres. Now you're responsible for setting up a database and getting it ready for the software to use.

Sure, you can run Postgres in Docker, and plenty of projects recommend it. But now you have two dependencies. If you don't already have Docker, you have to install it, which can mean a VM and a daemon on your machine. Then you have to run Postgres in it and make sure it's running whenever you use the software. That's a lot just to try something you don't know you want yet.

Wouldn't it be great to have the SQLite experience, but with Postgres?

That's miniPG. It isn't Postgres as a library. There's already a WASM project for that, reasonably called PGlite. miniPG is closer to the SQLite CLI: a single program that embeds a full Postgres server and client, wrapped up so you can use it the way you'd use sqlite3. Point it at a path, that path becomes the database, and you can run queries against it right away. There's no server to set up or keep running.

Jumping into a new Postgres database to try something out or debug it is now easier than using Postgres in a Docker container, and you don't need Docker at all. And miniPG still provides a fully functional Postgres server for software that needs one. In many cases, you can just launch an open source program that looks for its Postgres config in the environment with miniPG.

miniPG in 30 seconds

miniPG comes as a single, self-contained executable. You can just point it at a directory and run a query. There's no server to start, nothing to configure, and the result comes back immediately.

minipg ./mydb "create table notes (id serial, body text)"
minipg ./mydb "insert into notes (body) values ('hello')"
minipg ./mydb "select * from notes"

That directory is the database. When nothing is using it, it's just files on disk. You can copy it, back it up, or delete it.

This is actually real Postgres, not a compatibility layer, and the same binary runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.

When some software expects a Postgres server, miniPG can be one:

minipg serve ./mydb -p 5432

Like I mentioned before, it can even launch programs with environment variables that configure it for this Postgres database:

minipg run ./mydb -- some-tool

When the program is terminated, there's no database daemon to leave around or remember to stop. Only the data itself is kept right there on disk, ready to be used next time.

Instructions for getting it and even an interactive demo are available on the miniPG website.

Who is it for?

Software people, from developers to open source power users, and agents too, can use miniPG whenever they'd reach for SQLite but need Postgres.

  • Running software that only supports Postgres. This is what got me started. Self-hosting a tool shouldn't always mean operating a database server first.
  • Embedding Postgres in your own programs. If your tool needs Postgres, and PGlite doesn't cut it, you can ship and use miniPG. Users who don't care won't have to think about it, and users who want control can use it like sqlite3 to work with their data.
  • SQLite-style apps that need Postgres features. JSONB, full text search, window functions, extensions like pgvector or PostGIS. Postgres does so much more than SQLite, but it often wasn't worth the dependency.
  • Learning and experimenting with Postgres. No server, no config. Point it at a directory and start typing SQL.
  • Tests, local dev, and agents. A throwaway database per test, or a local copy of the same database you run in production, without Docker. Agents can spin up a real Postgres for a task and throw it away when they're done.

This really makes Postgres more viable for scenarios it wasn't before. I'd love to hear the use cases I haven't thought of.

Embedding Real Postgres

miniPG is the result of several attempts at embedding real Postgres into a standalone, cross platform binary.

Attempt 1: PGlite

The obvious place to start was PGlite. The name says it all, and in a sense it delivers: it's Postgres compiled to WebAssembly. In Go, you can load the module with the wazero runtime, run Postgres inside your program, and have your app connect to it. That's very close to the SQLite library experience.

Brad Fitzpatrick even made a proof of concept that does this in a way that makes PGlite work as a driver for the standard Go SQL package.

The catch is that PGlite only supports a single connection and a single session. Software written for a real Postgres server often assumes it can have more. A common pattern is to start a transaction, then make another query on a separate connection before committing. With only one connection, that second query waits for a transaction that's waiting on it. The app I was trying to run deadlocked.

Attempt 2: a VM in a webview

If I needed real Postgres, I could run real Postgres in a virtual machine I could embed. I have a soft spot for using webviews as portable containers, so I ran v86, an x86 emulator for the browser, inside one, and booted a full Postgres server in it.

The rest was plumbing. The headless webview opens a WebSocket back to the host program. Postgres connections are tunneled through it, and Postgres writes its data to a mount served over the same socket. The benefit of this approach is whatever platform the host program runs on, Postgres is always the same build running in the same VM.

I even built webframe for this, a library and CLI for running a native system webview headlessly.

The result was a proof of concept I called postgres-standalone: one binary, any platform, give it a port and a data directory, and you get a full Postgres server. It worked!

However, it was also an order of magnitude slower than native. Postgres in a VM in WebAssembly in a browser. Initializing and checking a database took a while. In the best case, on my M3 MacBook, it took 7 seconds before it would accept a connection.

I'd already written a design doc for the SQLite-style CLI: give it a directory, run a query, no server to run. On this stack, though, every SELECT * would sit there for 7 seconds first. That ruins the experience, so I had to shelve it. I had proven that embeddable Postgres was possible, just not pleasant.

Attempt 3: Hyper9

Later, for unrelated reasons, I built Hyper9. Inspired by system API translation, an approach that Wine and Valve's Proton are built on, combined with a unique way to use hypervisors, Hyper9 lets you run Plan 9 executables at near native speed on all platforms.

I'll be posting more about Plan 9 soon, but with a little extra magic, I was able to run the same Postgres at near native speed, in isolation, on all platforms. It's effectively the same approach as the previous attempt, but now without the slowdown.

Startup went from 7 seconds to 800ms. So I dusted off the design doc and built it. PGlite was taken, so postgres-standalone became miniPG.

What it isn't

miniPG isn't a replacement for real Postgres deployments. If you're running in the cloud, using replicas, or serving many users over many connections, use Postgres the normal way.

miniPG is for local, single-user programs: the places SQLite would fit, but you need Postgres.

That said, go ahead and see how far you can push it!

Try it

I'd really like to see how miniPG holds up in the wild, especially across different platforms and architectures. Please try it and tell me what breaks.

If this works, it proves a model that goes well beyond Postgres: taking complicated systems and packaging them as a single binary for more specific use cases. That's the part I find most exciting, and it's one of many new possibilities Hyper9 enables.

item.title: The dotfs protocol for 9P
item.description: A family of progressive protocol extensions for 9P
item.content:encoded:
Nov 19, 2026 · Jeff Lindsay, h.d.a.

Summary

The dotfs protocol (9p-dotfs in full) is four small, independent extensions a 9P server can expose as synthetic files under .fs/. A server implements only the ones it needs, and a client discovers each one by whether its file exists.

Extension File What it gives a client Useful alone for
Index .fs/index the whole tree's metadata in one read caching metadata of read-only trees, the .h9index use case
Events .fs/events a stream of changes after a sequence number inotify-style watching of any mutable server
Path operations .fs/ctl mv, rm, mkdir, cp, and flag changes by path, optionally conditional on a version quick operations without walk, open, and clunk sequences, and cross-directory rename on plain 9P2000
Staged commit .fs/stage/ plus commit on ctl resumable uploads published atomically if a path is still at an expected version conflict-safe writes

Together, index, events, path operations, and staged commit are enough to build a Dropbox-style synced folder, with one server ordering every change (the sync profile below), but nothing in the first three depends on sync.

The protocol works over any 9P transport. 9P2000.L over a WebSocket is the expected transport for browser clients, with authentication on the HTTP upgrade. This document is separate from hyper9's mount-index proposal and does not change it.

Conventions

These rules apply to every extension.

Location and scope

  • .fs/ lives at the top of an attach root. A directory may carry its own .fs/ (see nested indexes); everything in that .fs/ is scoped to that directory's subtree.
  • .fs/ is synthetic. It is never listed in its own index, never reported in events, and cannot be removed or renamed.
  • A server that implements none of the extensions has no .fs/. Clients must treat Enotfound on any .fs/ file as "not supported" and fall back to plain 9P.

Discovery

A client walks to .fs/ and reads the directory. Each extension is present if and only if its file is: index, events, ctl, stage/. ctl additionally answers caps with the commands it accepts, so a server can offer path operations without staged commit.

Paths

  • Paths are absolute from the scope root and use /. The scope root itself is /.
  • In every line format, bytes outside printable ASCII, space, %, and the newline are percent-escaped (%20). Every valid name can be listed, so there is no !unindexed.

Versions and sequence numbers

  • A scope with events or staged commit has a seq: an unsigned 64-bit counter that increases by one on every change in the scope.
  • A path's version is the seq of its last change; 0 means the path does not exist.
  • A server with an index but no events (a read-only tree) may report version 0 for every path and a fixed seq.
  • 9P qid.vers carries the low 32 bits of the version.

Line formats

Index lines, event records, and ctl commands are UTF-8 text, one record per line, fields separated by single spaces, unknown trailing fields ignored. A - stands for an empty field. Optional key=value fields may follow the positional ones.

ctl exchange

A client writes one command per Twrite to an open ctl fid, then reads the reply from the same fid before writing again. Replies start with ok or with an error word (conflict, missing, denied, invalid). Different fids are independent, so a client opens one ctl fid per concurrent operation.

Errors

Normal 9P errors (Rerror or Rlerror) report transport and permission failures. Protocol outcomes that a client acts on, such as a version conflict, are reply words on ctl rather than 9P errors.

Extension 1: index

.fs/index is a read-only snapshot of every path in the scope at one seq, so a client can answer walks, stats, and directory reads without asking the server.

Format

fsindex 1 seq <N> [<encoding>]
<path> <type> <mode> <length> <mtime> <version> <hash> <flags> [<target>] [key=value...]
...

fsindex 1 seq 48211
/ d 0755 0 1763491200 48000 - -
/.config d 0755 0 1763491100 47950 - p
/.config/git/config f 0644 212 1763400000 31002 b3:5e1a… p
/Documents/Tax%202025.pdf f 0644 284113 1763480011 46990 b3:9f2c… -
/Photos d 0755 0 1763491000 48100 - i
/bin l 0777 7 1763000000 120 - - usr/bin
Field Meaning
path escaped path from the scope root; lines sorted by path in byte order
type d directory, f file, l symlink
mode permission bits, octal
length bytes; 0 for directories, target length for symlinks
mtime seconds since the epoch
version see Conventions; 0 allowed for read-only trees
hash <algo>:<hex> content hash for files (b3 is BLAKE3-256), or -
flags -, or a set of letters: p prefetch, i nested index
target symlink target, escaped, only for type l

Reading

  • The header line is always plain text. Before reading, a client may write accept <encoding> [...] to the index fid; the server then may name one of them as the header's last word and send the rest of the file in that encoding. zstd (one frame) is the only encoding defined. With no accept, the body is plain, so cat .fs/index works.
  • The snapshot is consistent at seq N: every line reflects the scope after change N and before change N+1.
  • qid.vers of .fs/index is the low 32 bits of N, and its qid.path is stable, so a client can tell from Tstat whether a cached copy is current.
  • Length in Tstat may be 0 when the server generates the file on open.

Nested indexes (flag i)

A directory flagged i has its own .fs/ with its own index (and, if the server supports them, its own events and ctl). The parent's index lists the directory itself but none of its children, and versions inside are scoped to it. Use it for very large or busy subtrees, or for a different server mounted under a path. A client reads a nested index the first time it needs anything inside.

Prefetch (flag p)

A hint that a client keeping a local copy should fetch the file's content right after reading the index. On a directory it covers everything below. It is advisory and shared by all clients; per-device pinning is a client matter.

Read-only servers

A server with only an index (like a package cache) may use version 0, a fixed seq, and - for hashes and flags. That is exactly the role /.h9index plays today.

Extension 2: events

.fs/events streams change records for the scope, so a client can watch a tree like inotify without polling, with or without an index.

Opening a stream

Each open fid is its own stream. Before the first read a client may write any of:

Write Effect
since <N> start with the first change after seq N
path <dir> only report changes at or below <dir> (repeatable)
coalesce allow the server to merge consecutive changes to one path into the latest

Without since, the first record is seq <current> and only later changes follow.

Reading

Each Tread returns one or more whole records and blocks while there are none. A pending read is the push channel; Tflush cancels it. A record never spans two reads.

Records

<seq> put <index line>
<seq> del <path> [key=value...]
<seq> mv <from> <to> [key=value...]
<seq> flags <path> <flags> [key=value...]
<seq> reset

48212 put /Notes/todo.md f 0644 830 1763491250 48212 b3:77d0… p dev=mac-a1
48213 del /Downloads/old.zip dev=linux-b2
48214 mv /Draft.md /Posts/Final.md dev=mac-a1
48215 flags /Projects p dev=mac-a1
  • put is a create or modify and carries the whole index line, so a client never needs a follow-up stat.
  • mv of a directory moves everything below it; there is no record per child.
  • dev=<id> names the client that made the change, when known.
  • Records arrive in seq order. With coalesce a client may see gaps in seq; without it there are none.

Falling behind

A server keeps a bounded log. If since N names a seq it no longer has, or a reader falls too far behind, the server sends <seq> reset and ends the stream; the client must re-read the index (or simply rescan) and reopen with since.

Bootstrapping with an index

Two gap-free ways: read the index at seq N, then open events with since N; or open events first (getting seq <current>), read the index at some M, and drop records at or below M.

Extension 3: path operations

ctl performs namespace operations by path in one round trip, optionally conditional on a version. It needs no index or events, though a server with events reports every change it makes.

Commands

Command Effect Replies
caps lists supported commands ok <command>...
hello <device-id> names this client in events (dev=) ok
mkdir <path> [<base>] creates a directory ok <version>, conflict <version>
rm <path> [<base>] removes a file, symlink, or empty directory ok <seq>, conflict <version>, missing
rmtree <path> [<base>] removes a directory and everything below it ok <seq>, conflict <version>, missing
mv <from> <to> [<base>] [<tobase>] renames, across directories, atomically ok <version>, conflict <version>, missing
cp <from> <to> [<tobase>] copies on the server; cheap when content is deduplicated ok <version>, conflict <version>, missing
flags <path> <flags> sets the index flags (p, i) ok <version>
stat <path> returns the path's index line ok <index line>, missing

Conditional operations

  • <base> is the version the client expects <path> (or <from>) to have; <tobase> is the expected version of the destination, 0 meaning it must not exist.
  • If a base is given and does not match, nothing changes and the reply is conflict <current-version>.
  • Omitted bases make the operation unconditional, as with plain 9P.
  • A server without versions (no events, no staged commit) rejects any base with invalid.

Why this exists

  • 9P2000 wstat can only rename within one directory, so a cross-directory move otherwise means copy plus delete. 9P2000.L has Trenameat, but it is not conditional.
  • Path operations need no walk, open, and clunk sequence, which matters over high-latency WebSockets.
  • A conditional rm or mv lets a client act without racing another client's change.

Extension 4: staged commit

Staged commit lets a client upload a file's bytes over any number of connections and attempts, then publish them atomically at a path only if that path is still at the version the client expects.

Staging

  • A client creates a file under .fs/stage/ with any name it chooses (a UUID is recommended) and writes bytes at any offsets. Re-opening an existing stage file and writing more resumes an interrupted upload.
  • Stage files are private to the attaching user and invisible in the index and events.
  • A server removes stage files that have not been written for a period it chooses, at least one hour.

Publishing

Command Effect Replies
commit <stage> <path> <base> <mtime> <mode> [hash=<hash>] publishes the stage file at <path> if it is at <base>, then removes the stage file ok <version> <hash>, conflict <version>, invalid
commit-hash <hash> <path> <base> <mtime> <mode> publishes content the server already holds, with no upload ok <version>, conflict <version>, missing
abort <stage> discards a stage file ok
  • <base> is required, 0 for a new path. There is no unconditional commit; plain 9P writes serve that role.
  • With hash=, the server verifies the content and replies invalid on a mismatch.
  • The publish is atomic: other clients see either the old content or the new, never a mix.
  • commit-hash answers missing when the server lacks the content; the client then stages and commits normally. A server decides how widely it searches (one scope, or every scope of the same user); see Security considerations.

Ordering guarantee

On a server with events, the put record for a commit is assigned before the ok reply is sent, and the reply carries that version. A client therefore recognizes its own change in the stream by version, and never mistakes it for a remote edit.

Plain writes

A server with staged commit should still accept ordinary 9P writes. They apply as last-writer-wins when the fid is clunked and produce events like any other change.

Profiles

A profile is a named set of extensions plus the behavior a client can expect. Servers state the profiles they meet; the reference implementation meets all three.

Profile Extensions Typical server
Read-only cache index package and image caches such as wanix-cache
Watchable index (optional), events, path operations a mutable file server that other tools watch
Sync index, events, path operations, staged commit a server holding user roots for synced folders

Sync, as a composition (non-normative)

A sync client keeps a local copy of a scope and needs nothing beyond the four extensions:

  1. Bootstrap: hello, read the index with accept zstd, store every entry, then fetch content for p files not already held locally by hash.
  2. Follow: open events since <N>. Apply put, del, mv, and flags to the local copy; a changed hash makes a local copy stale.
  3. Write: remember the version a local edit started from. Publish with commit (or commit-hash first), and use conditional rm and mv for deletes and renames.
  4. Conflict: on conflict, keep the server's copy at the path, rename the local copy to name.sync-conflict-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>-<device>.ext, and commit it as a new file with base 0. A delete that conflicts with an edit loses, so the edit stays.
  5. Offline: queue changes with their base versions and replay them in order on reconnect.
  6. Reset: on a reset record, re-read the index and reconcile.

Because the server assigns one version per path, this needs no version vectors, and every change reaches every connected client in one round trip. The first commit to arrive wins, which is deterministic and never loses the other side's work.

Future extension: history (sketch)

A server that keeps old content and does not trim its log can expose past states with one more read-only extension, and no git-style checkout is needed: every seq already names a consistent state of the scope, so a past state can simply be served as a tree.

  • .fs/at/<seq>/ is a read-only view of the scope as it was right after change <seq>, with its own .fs/index at that seq. .fs/at/<timestamp>/ (RFC 3339) resolves to the last seq at or before that time.
  • history <path> on ctl lists a path's versions, newest first, as <version> <mtime> <hash> <op> dev=<id> lines.
  • Restore is an ordinary commit. cp /.fs/at/46990/Documents/Tax%202025.pdf /Documents/Tax%202025.pdf <base> copies an old version over the current one with a base version, so it goes through conflict detection and reaches every client as a normal put. With content deduplicated by hash, the copy costs nothing.
  • Retention is the server's policy (for example, every version for 30 days, then daily). .fs/at/<seq> answers Enotfound once a state is pruned.

Branches, merges, and per-client checkouts stay out of scope; the sketch only covers browsing and restoring the single line of history the server already orders. It needs nothing from the other extensions beyond what they define, so it can be added later without changing them.

Security considerations

The protocol adds no authentication of its own; it relies on the transport and on 9P's per-attach identity, and adds a few concerns to handle.

  • Authentication. Over WebSocket, authenticate on the HTTP upgrade (cookie or bearer token) and map that to the attach user. 9P Tauth is not used. Raw TCP transports should be limited to localhost or wrapped in TLS.
  • Scope. Every .fs/ file and command is limited to the attach root. Paths in ctl are resolved within the scope, and .. never leaves it.
  • Hash probing. commit-hash and cp reveal whether the server holds some content. A server must only consider content the attaching user can already read, so a user cannot learn about another user's files.
  • Metadata exposure. The index exposes every name in the scope at once. A server must only serve indexes of scopes the user can fully read, or leave unreadable subtrees out.
  • Resource limits. Servers should cap index size, the number of open event streams per user, stage space per user, and ctl command length, and return denied or a 9P error when a limit is hit.
  • Event retention. The log reveals recent names, including of deleted files, to anyone who can read the scope; keep the retention window no longer than needed.

Relation to mount-index

The index extension is a deliberate iteration on /.h9index, but the mount-index proposal stays unchanged until this is proven. If it is later folded in:

/.h9index today .fs/index
Location /.h9index at the root .fs/index, alongside the other extensions
Names with spaces or non-UTF-8 left out, directory marked !unindexed percent-escaped, always listed
qid.vers of entries 0 the path's version, or 0 for read-only trees
Changes regenerate the file the events extension
Content identity none optional hash per file
Hints none p prefetch, i nested index
Encoding plain text plain, or zstd after an opt-in

Prior art

System What this borrows
Coda (CMU, from AFS) disconnected operation: a log of local changes replayed with conflict detection
Plan 9 replica(1) a database of paths plus a change log to bring a copy up to date
Upspin Watch(name, sequence), a change stream after a sequence number
Dropbox API v2 snapshot with a cursor, deltas, and a long-poll to block; hash dedupe; resumable uploads
WebDAV sync-collection (RFC 6578), Nextcloud sync tokens for deltas; If-Match compare-and-swap writes
Syncthing BEP index and index updates keyed by sequence; conflict-copy naming
inotify, fanotify event vocabulary for local watching

These are from memory; links and checks against each system's documentation are still to add.

Open questions

  • Is one snapshot per scope fine at user-data scale (about 100 bytes a line, roughly 10 MB uncompressed for 100k files), with nested indexes only for large subtrees?
  • Should events offer an index diff for a client slightly behind, or is since N always enough?
  • Should ignore rules (temp files, .DS_Store) be part of the protocol, for example as a flag or a shared file, or left to clients?
  • Is hello worth keeping, or should the device id come from the transport?
  • Which hash algorithms are allowed besides BLAKE3, and is the hash ever required?

item.title: Background
item.description: An old bio of Jeff Lindsay, originally from the old progrium.com website and blog.
item.content:encoded:
Jeff Lindsay is a systems thinking hacker-philosopher. He builds, he explores, and is apparently "wired differently." Obsessed with esoteric knowledge, he applies modern technology driven by an eclectic model of the bigger picture. He's heavily involved in hacker culture, startup culture, web technologies and the indie game scene.

While freelancing in 2005, Jeff met David Weekly, a local hacker-entrepreneur that later founded PBworks. Together they started a free and open monthly event called SuperHappyDevHouse, "a party for hackers and thinkers." It quickly gained the attention of the Silicon Valley digerati and inspired other events such as BarCamp and Yahoo! Hack Day, as well as a network of SHDH-modeled events in countries around the world. The original SHDH event has been featured in the San Jose Mercury News, SFGate, and CNET News.com, and courted by tech giants such as Google and Sun.

After years of hobby game development, Jeff met freeware game developer Derek Yu in 2005 and helped him run and develop a blog called TIGSource. The Independent Game Source has grown into a major community that helped bring about what is now called the indie game scene, the source of hits such as Fez, Super Meat Boy, Spelunky, World of Goo, Braid, and even Minecraft. The TIGSource community has become part of a loose network of indie game developers, overlapping with many involved in the IGF and GDC. TIGSource has been championed by many in the game industry including 1UP, Kotaku, and Penny Arcade.

While working on a startup in 2006, Jeff wrote about a pattern in web architecture he called "webhooks". Jeff has since presented about webhooks at Glue Conference, SXSW, and for Google and Pivotal Labs tech talks. Jeff's work has led to the adoption of webhooks by Google, GitHub, PBworks, SocialText and many others. In 2009, the pattern was used in a protocol called PubSubHubbub, used to make RSS and Atom feeds real-time. Jeff is a contributor to PubSubHubbub, which has been deployed by Google, Six Apart, FriendFeed and others. Jeff has also developed many tools and open source software to support a webhooks ecosystem, including RequestBin and Localtunnel.

The success of SuperHappyDevHouse led to the formation of Hacker Dojo, a non-profit community center for technologists. Jeff co-founded Hacker Dojo in 2009 with SuperHappyDevHouse co-founder David Weekly and a group of passionate friends from the community, including Lee Felsenstein, moderator of the 1970's computer hobbyist group Homebrew Computer Club. In just three months of operating with over 100 paying members and hundreds of visitors for events and coworking, Hacker Dojo achieved immediate success. Hacker Dojo made headlines on the front page of the Mercury News and garnered a letter of congratulations from the City of Mountain View.

Over the years, Jeff has worked with various startups and organizations as a software developer or advisor, including CommerceNet, Netflix, NASA Ames, and Twilio.

Full Article (7min)

Proposals, Not Milestones

I've started a new primitive called hyper9 , initially as an experiment to see how far I could push working with coding agents. It's ambitious and exciting, and right now it's in a pretty good place. Though, maybe halfway to a real v0.1 release. Getting to this point with it forced me to finally solve a problem I've had with projects like this for a long time.

For day-to-day work we have todos, milestones, and sprints, and those work fine when we're actively in that mode. minipg v0.3

item.title: 🛠️ tailcat: Tailscale without Tailscale, by Tailscale ↗
item.content:encoded:
tailcat: Tailscale without Tailscale, by Tailscale

tailcat is netcat over Tailscale's data plane without its control plane. One side listens and gets a short address, the other connects to it, and traffic flows over end-to-end WireGuard tunnels that bootstrap through DERP and then hole-punch to direct UDP when they can. Connection metadata is exchanged out of band however you like, so there's no Tailscale account, no root, and no changes to routing or DNS. It ships as both a CLI and a Go library.

item.title: Proposals, Not Milestones
item.content:encoded:
I've started a new primitive called hyper9, initially as an experiment to see how far I could push working with coding agents. It's ambitious and exciting, and right now it's in a pretty good place. Though, maybe halfway to a real v0.1 release. Getting to this point with it forced me to finally solve a problem I've had with projects like this for a long time.

For day-to-day work we have todos, milestones, and sprints, and those work fine when we're actively in that mode. But my open source projects with larger arcs, and ideas that need a lot of thought before I can build them (let alone anybody else), have always been missing something. It turns out I already knew what it was: a written proposal process, sometimes called ADRs. They've been very effective working with coding agents, but also, having coding agents has finally made the process practical for me.

The usual loop

Working with coding agents, I've settled into a plan-then-implement rhythm. I'll write a rough sketch prompt, then have the LLM turn it into a PLAN that's sort of like a spec. I review it, modify it, and then tell the agent to implement it.

From there it usually drifts out of sync, because there's no formal process. Sometimes when things are roughly done, I'll have the agent convert the PLAN into an updated DESIGN or SPEC that lives with the code, so there's some kind of design documentation and history. Other times I don't even keep the PLAN around. I just make commits and iterate forward.

For most projects so far that's been okay. Many open source projects, and some of my bigger projects usually ask you to "submit an issue before a PR" so there's a chance to talk about the design first. That's a hint at what's missing: a place for the design to be discussed and decided before anyone writes code. Not just initially, but throughout development.

How hyper9 started

hyper9 began the way most of my projects do lately: chatting with ChatGPT on my phone, notebook in hand. I put the idea together in my head, did research, and validated assumptions. Eventually I said "draft a design doc," and that became the working design document until implementation started.

The project was too big for a single plan, so the doc broke it into milestones. Each milestone was a collection of things. The early ones were small, but they got bigger and bigger. Though, you wouldn't notice it by looking at the words.

I should have seen the problem coming when I started doing "milestone prep." Before taking on M3, I'd ask what needed to happen first. That turned into a planning step of its own, full of unlisted work: set up a test harness, do some prerequisite work, answer some open questions. Once that was done, I could usually turn the milestone over to the agent to implement on its own.

Stuck in research mode

As the project grew, the milestones I'd defined upfront grew too. Sometimes after prep and planning, the agent would just read files and look things up for 30 minutes. One time I left it for over two hours, and it still hadn't written anything. It was all reading source and researching, which does go into its context and makes for a better implementation.

It was funny, it was like a new junior programmer too afraid to start because they don't feel prepared. Safer to just keep learning.

The real issue was that the milestones were too big. They were one-liners like "M4: this, this, this, and this. Should be able to X." Each of those "this" items probably deserved its own plan.

Patching the process

This time I did one thing right: I had the agent keep the overall plan, which had become DESIGN, up to date. Whenever planning or implementing a milestone surfaced something that would change or add to the design, the agent updated the doc. It also added a short entry to a Milestone Changelog section, recording what changed and why, grouped by milestone.

That worked, but then dependencies showed up. Dependencies were how the milestones got ordered in the first place, and new discoveries could change that order.

Then I started running work in parallel. A milestone plan would lay out steps, and if one could be done independently, I'd have another agent session take it. They usually touched different files, and occasional overlap was fine. But the DESIGN doc and its changelog became a shared hotspot that every session wanted to edit.

I originally had M0 through M10 milestones. I assumed the early ones would be the hardest, with all the setup and foundation work, and later ones would get easier as "just features." The opposite happened. The project got bigger and more complex, and the later milestones listed a bunch of pretty big things.

So I stopped at M4. It was a good point for validation and demos that showed, yes, this will work. And then I had the agent help me come up with a new process.

Enter proposals

I've always wanted to run a project on a written proposal system. The idea goes back to internet protocols and RFCs (Requests for Comments). Python has PEPs (Python Enhancement Proposals), and Go has its own proposal process. You get a written record of how an idea evolved: its design and its plan for implementation. You can collect comments and revise before approving and building it. And it lines up neatly with the plan-then-implement loop you already want with coding agents.

So I based hyper9's new process on Go's, with some modifications. Fittingly, the first proposal was for the proposal system itself: proposals.md explains the motivation, how it works, and how we migrated to it. The rules live in the design README.

The short version:

  • No more milestones. Each piece of work is its own proposal, a Markdown file in design/ covering design and planning.
  • Dependencies in frontmatter. Each proposal lists what it depends on, along with status and other bookkeeping. The order of work comes from the dependency graph, not a numbered sequence.
  • A clear workflow. A sketch becomes an initial proposal with open questions. Then there's room for discussion, a final comment period, and formal approval.
  • A tool that knows what's ready. It reports when a proposal is accepted and all its dependencies are implemented, so it's ready to build. It also validates the graph in CI and regenerates a status table in the project README.
  • GitHub issues for discussion. Filing a proposal opens an issue for open discussion and tracking. Revisions happen as commits to the doc.
  • DESIGN stays current. DESIGN.md now describes only what exists. The PR that finishes a proposal updates it.
  • A human signs off. Agents can help write proposals, but a named person has to direct, review, and sign the work.

The old M0 through M4 became a single "baseline" proposal marked implemented. The remaining milestones were split by feature into separate drafts.

Why it works

This solves the pre-development design process. It documents the thinking and the original plan, and it keeps the main design doc up to date as a current spec rather than a pile of plans.

It also makes open contributions easier, both for design and for the question "what's ready that I can help with?" And that applies to agents too. I can point an agent at a proposal to flesh it out, challenge it, or at another to implement it. I can point several agents at different proposals without them getting in each other's way on design, prep, and planning. Actual implementation happens in branches when needed.

This setup makes agent assisted human contribution easy, too. You can do the same thing I do: point your coding agent at a proposal, keep a loose eye on what it does, and review what it completes. Though, if you didn't write the proposal, it's probably a good idea to talk through it with the agent to better understand it.

The best part is that the formalisms, the design and customization of this workflow, but more importantly the work of actually following it are suddenly not overwhelming. Agents carry most of that load. A process like this would have felt like bureaucracy for a small project before. Now it's mostly free.

A real roadmap

hyper9 now has a real roadmap: proposals at various stages, each with a GitHub issue. Some are ready to start, and some are longer-term ideas still being developed. There are also a few unnumbered sketches in the design/ directory that don't have issues yet. A table in the project README, kept up to date by a tool, makes it easy to see what's ready to work on.

I can think through a bunch of ideas, load them in as proposals, and let them simmer and develop until I think they're ready to be implemented. It's not quite a software factory, but it definitely feels like an augmented assembly line. One where feel in control of the design, and make better design decisions.

item.title: 🛠️ isobox: Run a command in a sandbox, with the same flags on every OS ↗
item.content:encoded:
isobox: Run a command in a sandbox, with the same flags on every OS

isobox is a Go CLI that compiles one sandbox policy to each OS's native mechanism: Seatbelt on macOS, gVisor on Linux, and AppContainer on Windows. Instead of pretending every backend is equal, it uses an explicit capability model that flags where enforcement falls short, and a strict mode that refuses anything that isn't portable.

item.title: 📄 vx32: Lightweight User-level Sandboxing on the x86 ↗
item.content:encoded:
vx32: Lightweight User-level Sandboxing on the x86

Bryan Ford and Russ Cox's paper on sandboxing untrusted x86 code entirely in user space, with no kernel changes or special privileges. Vx32 confines guest memory access with segmentation and runs guest code through a dynamic translator that rewrites unsafe instructions, so most code runs close to native speed. Its applications include portable archive decoders and 9vx, which runs the Plan 9 kernel as an ordinary process on another OS.

item.title: 🛠️ hl: Run aarch64-linux ELF binaries on macOS Apple Silicon ↗
item.content:encoded:
hl: Run aarch64-linux ELF binaries on macOS Apple Silicon

hl runs Linux ELF binaries on Apple Silicon Macs without Docker or a full VM. Each process gets its own tiny Hypervisor.framework VM with a minimal kernel shim that traps Linux syscalls and hands them to the host, which translates about 170 of them to macOS equivalents. It handles static and dynamic binaries, threads, fork and exec, signals, and networking, and can run x86_64 binaries too by way of Rosetta.

webframe v0.2

webframe is now a tool for scripting and testing pages, not just watching them. You can inject stubs, run test files after load, pass in secrets, set timeouts, and let the page set the exit status, and hidden pages run unthrottled on every platform.

item.content:encoded:
webframe v0.1

The first release of webframe, which runs a web page like a program: it loads a URL in a hidden web view and wires its console to stdout, its exceptions to stderr, and stdin to a JavaScript REPL. It's a single ~5 MB binary that uses the webview your OS already has.

Wanix v0.4 Preview: Composable compute in HTML

Wanix Elements are web components for declaring filesystems, tasks, VMs, terminals, and even VS Code in plain HTML, so you can build a sandboxed Unix-style environment in the browser with a few tags. This preview also adds the rc shell and a Wanix-ready Alpine Linux as CDN extras.
